segments.text: If we can get settled, those that are seated behind, please let's fill up the seats in front of us. If there's an empty seat in front of you, please move in and fill up those spaces. May we settle down, please? Good morning and welcome to this session that is being hosted by Southern Africa.

Honorable Ministers present, Excellencies, Permanent Secretaries, Youth Innovators, Entrepreneurs, Policymakers, Distinguished Guests, and Development Partners, good morning. Welcome to a session that is a little different from the usual conference panel. Today, we are changing the rules.

Usually, young people are the ones that are invited to stand before audiences and policymakers and explain why they need jobs, why they need their hassles, their entrepreneurship ideas to be supported, why they need opportunities and support. But today, we have turned the tables. Our governments from within the region must speech to our young people and tell them what they have to offer.

Eight countries from Southern Africa will make their case this morning in the spirit of friendly competition to convince you whether their country is a strong place where a young entrepreneur can go and start a business, a trade, innovate, and build their future. Welcome to Pitch My Country session. My name is Mabobe Nnedziwe, Director Youth from the Ministry of Youth, Sport, and Arts in Zambia, your moderator this morning, and I will invite my co-moderator, a youth voice, to introduce herself.
Good morning, Africa. Good morning, Africa. Viva, youth, viva.
Viva, youth, viva. Viva, Africa, viva. Good morning.
The energy in the room should match the energy in Africa. My name is Hope Ezromkwinda, and I am the co-moderator. I am a youth advisory group member for the EQUIAD projects.

And I'm glad that I'm here on this stage. And one of the things that, for me, this is a 360 moment where I am on stage sharing a platform with one of my mentors in youth development. I'm glad to be here.
And let's have fun while we start it. And so, before we get into our session, we will have some music so that we can energize ourselves in the true spirit of Africanism. DJ, please.
Please be upstanding. For this one, we have to all stand. We need to stand.
Okay. Faster, faster, Gigi. Jerusalem, my world.
My world. Remember we taught the youth connect dance? Let's go. Let's go, the youth connect dance.

We are not seeing the energy, please, let's dance, here is the routine, let's dance. Come on Africa, you can do better than that, you can do better than that. I'm not seeing the honourable ministers dancing, I can't see you dancing.

Honourable ministers, please, we want to see the dancers. Your excellencies, we want to see the dancers. Imagine the way you are dancing, that is going to determine whether you get to win the beach or not.

Are you sure you are going to get it? Okay, let's do one more round, give it your energy, let's see your energy, yes. Let's do the electric slide. Yes, the judges in front are doing it, the judges in front are doing it, yes.
Yes, come on. Yes, that is the energy, come on. Yes, come on.
Come on. The honourables are doing it right in front. Come on, round of applause.
Come on. I can see the honourable minister is also doing it in his own way. I can see the honourable minister is also doing it in his own way.

How many of us are feeling more than youthful and energetic again this morning? Lovely, lovely. I was seeing our honourable ministers and permanent secretaries in front giving us their best, right? But on the next round, we will outdo them. Young people, I trust you.
Viva young people, viva. Great, that's amazing. So this lovely session is proudly convened by the Republic of Zambia.

Great, so it is proudly convened by Zambia in partnership with the United Nations Development Programme through the Enhancing Capacities of Women and Youth-Led Enterprises for Regional Trade Project, also known as the ICOAD project. And we are bringing together eight countries. How many are excited? Eight countries, that's exciting, right? And we have Botswana, Eswatini, Malawi, Namibia, Lesotho, South Africa, Zambia, Zimbabwe.

Which country have I left out? If you're in the house and I've left out your country, just shout it. Which country have I left out? We will get there. Thank you very much for being in the room and we believe that we are going to learn from you as well.

So during this morning, we are going to do this under the track three of YouthConnekt Africa Summit, which is beyond the paycheck, dignified work and livelihoods in the modern economy. If the economy is modern, its workforce has to be modern and the opportunities have to meet what is on the ground. Are you agreeing with me? So today, our central message today is very simple.
Young people are at the center of everything. A young person who can access only one market has limited opportunities. A young person who can access regional markets has a bigger future.

We don't want one opportunity. We want multiple opportunities. A bigger market for exports, imports and favorable policies that enable young people to trade without any obstacles, to be able to contribute to the sustainable development of their countries.

Young people, we no longer want to just be the menu on the table, but what we want is to bring the ingredients to the table so that we cook together with the older generation holding our hands. Are we together? Young people, does that look like what we need? Yeah, it's not what you need. You're not convincing enough.
Is that what we need? Yes. Great. Thank you very much.

So today, as we have spoken what we want, and as we are going to invite the countries, the people who are pitching their countries, we want the energy, but also what we want is what opportunities are you offering us in your country? How can we participate in development, even as young people? So as you come here, bring the energy. Yes, we love that, but also tell us where the opportunities lie. Tell us where you need us to also benefit from the cake of the nation.
Thank you very much. I will hand over to my co-moderator. Thank you so much, Hope.
And so before we get into the protocols, I would like to recognize our youth advisory group, our jury for today. Please, a round of applause for them. So we mean serious business.

As the countries come up here to pitch their countries, you need to put your best foot forward because we do have a jury, and it's a youth jury. So you need to make sure that even as you pitch, you have that in mind. I also want to recognize MasterCard Foundation for the role that they continue to play in supporting youth development matters.

With that said, it is my singular honor and rare opportunity to call upon the Minister of Youth, Sport and Arts from Zambia to come and give us the keynote address. Honorable Minister. Thank you very much.

I was almost now dancing because those are the ones we dance ourselves. Thank you so very much. Moderators, Program Director, Distinguished Ministers, Permanent Secretaries and Head of Delegation from Botswana, Malawi, Namibia, South Africa, Zimbabwe, and the Kingdom of Eswatini, not forgetting Sudan.

Is it Sudan or South Sudan? Sudan. Thank you so very much. May I also recognize the presence of representatives of the United Nations Development Program and the EcoYate Regional Project, members of EcoYate Youth Advisory Group, development partners, young entrepreneurs, innovators, and ladies and gentlemen.
Good afternoon. Is it afternoon or is it still morning? It's still morning. It's a great honor to join you at the Southern Africa Regional Session of the 2026 YouthConnekt Africa Summit.

First and foremost, allow me to commend the Government of Rwanda, the YouthConnekt Africa Secretariat, my Zambian team, UNDP, the EcoYate Regional Project, and all partners for creating this important platform that places young people at the center of Africa's development agenda. Africa's greatest asset is in its youthful population. Our future prosperity will depend on how effectively we invest in young people by equipping them with skills, opportunities, and enabling environment to innovate, trade, and lead.

The African continent free trade area presents an unprecedented opportunity. Beyond being a trade agreement, the African continent free trade area is a catalyst for economic transformation, enabling youth-led enterprises to access regional and continental markets. However, many young entrepreneurs continue to face barriers, including limited access to finance, market information, technology, and cross-border business opportunities.

It is our collective responsibility to remove these barriers. Today's speech, my country session, represents an important shift in thinking. Rather than asking young people to justify their potential, governments are challenged to demonstrate how they are creating opportunities for the youth to succeed.

This is the right approach because young people are not beneficiaries of development, but rather drivers. For Zambia, youth empowerment is a national investment. We remain committed to expanding access to skills, entrepreneurship, technology, finance, and markets through strong partnerships with the private sector, development partners, and civil society.

Particular attention is being given to the young women, youth-led enterprises, and young people in rural communities, and those with disabilities, so that no one is left behind. As Southern African countries, our greatest strength lies in collaboration. By sharing experiences, strengthening regional partnerships, and supporting cross-border entrepreneurship, we can build an integrated regional economy where young innovators and businesses thrive beyond national boundaries.

To the young people gathered here today, your ideas, innovation, and leadership are essential to Africa's future. Continue to ask bold questions, challenge us to do better, and see the opportunities before you. As I conclude, I wish to echo that.

Let us reaffirm our shared commitment to creating an Africa where regional integration expands opportunity, entrepreneurship creates jobs, innovation drives prosperity, and every young person has the chance to thrive. Together, let us shape a future worthy of Africa's next generation. I thank you all.

Thank you for those amazing remarks. I have caught something very important that he has spoken about, and one of them is shared commitment. Where I come from in Zambia, there is a proverb in Bemba that means, It simply means, one firewood cannot make the fire burn.

So it is in that regard that, at this point, I would want us to hear some remarks as well from our development partner. It is shared commitments like our Honorable Minister has said. From development, either at social enterprises or whichever sector of the government, we are constantly working with development partners.

And it is in that regard that I'm going to call upon the Deputy Resident Representative from UNDP to just come up here and give us some remarks. A round of applause for him, please. A round of applause, young people.
Thank you very much. Thank you so much. I love this kind of energy for the young people.

And as you can see, I'm among the young people. So I try to color my hair so that, but I'm still young, right? Honorable Ricardo Mufalari, Minister of Youth, Sports and Arts, Zambia. Honorable Pizzo Lesaona, Minister of Gender, Youth and Social Development, Lesotho.

Ms. Natasha Rampa, P.S., Minister of Youth and Gender, Botswana. My good friend, Kango Chileshe, P.S., Minister of Youth and Sports and Arts, Zambia. Mr. Jameson Nalama, Secretary, Minister of Youth and Sports and Culture, Malawi.

Mr. Salomon Mlanga, P.S., Minister of Youth and Employment Development and Vocational Training, Zimbabwe. Mr. Luassi Mamba, CEO, Eswatini National Youth Council, Kingdom of Eswatini. Mrs. Judith Msousa, Director, Minister of Youth, Sports and Culture, Malawi.

Rhoda Gadama, CEO, National Youth Council of Malawi. Emmanuel Ganak, Director, Youth Legislation and Policy Department of Women, People with Disabilities, South Africa. Mr. David Gawasem, Senior Youth Officer, MESFIN, Comas Regional Council, Namibia.

Without forgetting my very good friend, I know he doesn't like it, but MESFIN. Can you just stand and say hi to this beautiful audience? MESFIN is the engineering of this youthful project. MESFIN works for Masakar Foundation.

He is someone who is very deep in terms of analyzing the portfolio management of this good project. Which for us, I think, is a proof of concept in the Southern Africa region, where Masakar Foundation really comes to apply the African free trade that we are talking, politicians are talking. But this is a good example.

Thank you for being with us on these pitch exercises. So, ECOYAT regional team, country coordinator, we thank you for really coming here in Kigali. Member of the project, member of youth advisory group, we thank you.
Without you, we cannot do anything. You need to advise us. Young entrepreneur and innovator, development partner, dear ladies and gentlemen.

I'm so happy, and this is my great pleasure, really, to welcome you in this high-level Southern Africa regional session, Pitch Your Country, 2026 YouthConnekt Africa. Allow me to extend my great thanks to the government of Rwanda for hosting us, and especially the government of Zambia, represented by the Honorable Minister, for co-hosting this session. We don't take it for granted, the Honorable Minister.

And for your continued commitment, and all government leaders from the countries that are supported by ECOYAT, your presence here gives us a deep understanding that the government, the respected government, is at the heart of this good initiative. I wish to commend the project, for those who don't know what ECOYAT is, it's Enhancing Capacities of Women and Youth-Led Enterprises for Regional Trade. Let me also thank for the contribution to strengthen the youth entrepreneurship and regional trade across Southern Africa.

Through its work in Botswana, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Malawi, South Africa, Zambia and Zimbabwe, the ECOYAT project is helping young entrepreneurs to access markets, to access finance, and to get opportunities that are arising across Africa. So, today's session is more than a platform for presentations, as the moderator said. It's a unique opportunity for you.

It's a unique opportunity for dialogue between government and young people on what it takes to unlock economic opportunity at scale. Traditionally, young people are invited to listen. To policy announcements, to political talks about what government intends to do for them.
And most of the time, nothing happens right after. So, today, we want to change our way of doing business. We want to change the narrative, because this is your moment.
You young people need to recall that you are at the center of the conversation. This platform is not only about government speaking to youth. It is about government listening to the youth.
We want to hear your ideas. We want to hear your experience. Your aspirations and your solutions.

In particular, we must ensure that the voices of young women, who often face the greatest barriers in terms of opportunity. We want your participation. We want to hear about economic empowerment in the real world.
We want to hear and reflect the decision we make when you are talking. Again, to you, the young people. I think I'm among the young people, right? If you are alone.
Because I feel young this morning. To you, the young people in the room, take your place at the table. Speak boldly.
You have to speak. Don't be shy. You have to challenge us constructively.

You have to hold us accountable. The policies, the programs, and the investments that are designed for you young people will only succeed if they are informed by your realities and shaped by your voice. Let me just come back a year ago when we were discussing the Mastercard Foundation about this program.

I do recall that one of the prerequisites was to create the YAC, the Youth Advisory Group. Because they said, why are you talking on behalf of the young generation? Let them speak. That's why, as we are implementing this project, this proof of concept is a proof of concept in the Southern Africa region.
You have to challenge us as we move on. If you have an action plan that is not in line with the aspiration of the young people, stop us. Reflect before we move.

So I'm really delighted, again, to welcome the participating governments of Zambia, Namibia, Botswana, Malawi, Zimbabwe, South Africa, and Eswatini. And maybe Sudan, if you challenge us as you should, right? Today, each country brings its strength, experience, opportunity that can inspire young people and foster greater regional collaboration. Most importantly, this session is not only about showcasing national achievements.

No, it's about exploring how our countries can work together to create a more integrated and inclusive regional economy. I think it's all about this YouthConnekt gathering here. What are we learning from each other? And the ECOWAS programme is all about that.
It has this regional characteristic. It's six countries, but it can go beyond. It depends.

And remember, I told you, for us who are in the development space, this is the very first concrete activity in terms of implementation of the African continental trade. And this is targeting the young generation, 85% of young women. So young women, please open the eyes, challenge us.

This is for you, from 15 to 35. Don't ask to be my age, but I'm just giving you the bracket, 15 years to 35, and most of you are in that bracket. We, as a United Nations Development Programme, UNDP, we remain committed to working alongside with the governments, regional institutions, the private sector, and young people to make trade more inclusive, entrepreneurship more productive, and economic opportunity more accessible.

Together, we must ensure that the AFCTA is not merely a continental agreement, but a catalyst for real opportunity experienced by young people in their business, in their community, and every life. Your Excellencies, distinguished young leaders, let me again warmly welcome all of you. Your presence here reflects our shared commitment to build a Southern Africa where young people can access dignified livelihoods, create enterprises, drive innovation, and contribute meaningfully to sustainable economic growth.

To our government representative here, we thank you again for your leadership and your efforts to create an enabling environment for youth development, economic participation. To you, the young people in this room, I encourage you to engage actively again. Ask bold questions, don't be shy, share your perspective, and seize this opportunity that emerged from today's discussion.
So within this remark, I just want to thank you for your attention. I know I've been a bit long, but I do believe that now the floor is for you. Challengers, this is your moment.
I thank you so much. A round of applause, please. A more energetic and youthful round of applause.
Yes, that's more like it. I love the shouts. That's what young people do, they shout, right? A round of applause as he takes his seat.
Young people, a round of applause. Great, great. That's more like it.

Thank you very much, GRR, for your special remarks. And one of the things that is emphasized on is us young people holding the older generation accountable for the things that they put in place for us to benefit from. So young people, for us to hold the older generation accountable, we must be willing to be guided by them.

Is that right? I know we're young people, but we still need the older generation, right? Even though he said he's younger. So I think we'll put up a challenge for him to see if he can dance as the young ones can. Yes, that's the word.

So at this point in time, we're going to welcome some not necessarily welcoming remarks because as young people, we're not into the speeches, we're more into the actions. So we're going to just hear a brief background, an overview of what the EcoYard project is, why are we here, and why is this program important to us as we sit in this room? At this point in time, help me welcome Miss Ethel Bangwayo, who is the regional project manager of the EcoYard. A round of applause.
Yags, I expect you to scream louder. Yes, thank you very much. I'm going to come here a bit closer.
Good morning, my name is Ethel Bangwayo. I am the regional project manager for the EcoYard project. Thank you to the DRR.

He's already started to explain what the project is about, but we thought this is a good opportunity, since you are here already, to hear a little bit about the project and how you can partner with us. We are working in the six countries that you've heard in southern Africa, but the reason we are here is to help women and youth-led enterprises to access regional value chains. Many of the young people who are here are running some sort of business, but there are challenges that you face in terms of how you run your business, how you access finance, even the ecosystem.

So those are the sort of issues that we are trying to address as EcoYard, under three broad categories. The first one, we work with you to tackle issues like, how do you manage your business? How do you make yourselves ready to access finance? Licensing. Who do you go to? Where? How? Who are the people you need to be partnering with? Where are they? Who can you group with? The market as well.

How do you access the market? Where is this market? And who else do you need to be working alongside for you to be able to access the market? What about the digital tools? More and more we see digital is important in enhancing our efficiency, in helping us to access those markets. We deal with issues like that. Under the second pillar, issues of access to finance, we know that accessing finance is difficult for young people and for women, even though we know, the research tells us, that women in particular, their default rates are lower, but somehow it's still difficult.
So we help you tackle issues like that. Then the last pillar is the ecosystem. This is why we have the ecosystem here.

The policy makers, regulators, sometimes those things get in the way. You've got the funding you need, you've got the capacities you need, but there's that policy that is getting in the way. There's that regulation that is getting in the way.

You get to the border, they are telling you things that don't make sense. As EcoYet, we want to work with you to engage together, policy makers, the regulators, but even the ecosystem. When you think about, for instance, the Chamber of Commerce in your country, who are the members? It's mainly older people, but not only that, it's the older men in their dark suits.

Do you feel like you belong there? Can you really belong and can you benefit? As EcoYet, we are wanting to tackle some of these issues. Our partners, we have some institutional partners we are working with, the Commissioner Federation for Women in Business, they are here, thank you very much for coming. We have the Trade and Development Fund, and we also have the Better Than Cash Alliance.

Together, over the next four or five years, maybe even more, Mesfin will let us know. If we impress them enough, maybe even longer, we can be here working with yourselves as young people. But of course, there's nothing that we do that can be effective for young people if we are not constantly hearing from them.
That's why we have our esteemed Youth Advisory Group. Please give them a round of applause. We love these people.
We love them so much. They keep us in check. They are that voice that is constantly in our ear, reminding us of what is relevant for young people and what young people respond to.

Thank you very much. Thank you so much, Ethel, for that overview on the EcoYet project. We are getting to that exciting moment, and I wish, as young people, you could see what I'm seeing in front here.

You know how we get anxious? For today, count me as one of you. You know how you get anxious before a jury, before a panel? You should see what I'm seeing in front here. And it's good that we've turned the tables so that we listen to them.

They are also under pressure, and so we are looking forward to see what they are going to do. And we also know that usually, usually our superiors are not good at keeping time. So today, one of the things that we are, especially the politicians, they can talk for the whole day.
And so, the countries have five minutes each to pitch. In five minutes, you will pitch. So I'm giving you the rules of the pitch.

So five minutes, you do your pitch. You pitch your country to us. And then also, as you do your pitch, we want to hear from you where the actual business and employment opportunities are for our young people, what support is available to the young entrepreneurs, and how they can access it.

Remember, I say that we do have a jury, so this is the leakage that I'm giving you. How can young people reach regional and continental markets in your respective countries? And what makes your country's offer distinctive and credible to the youth of Southern Africa gathered in here today? And so, after each pitch, after the pitch session, the audience will answer a simple question. Would I do business in this country? So remember that, even as you do your speech.

Our youth advisory group will serve as the jury, as Elia indicated, and they will assess the pitches and ask questions and deliver a youth-centered verdict. A round of applause to that. To our timekeeper, remember I said we have people that are not good at keeping time, so please, each country has five minutes.

And so, we are going to cross over now and start inviting our panelists to come up stage even as they pitch their countries. DJ, remember we need to have music. And also, as you dance, there's an award for the best dancer.

There's an award for the best dancer. As Africans, we are well known for dancing. So please, to those that are representing our respective countries, we are counting on you not to let us down because we will hold you accountable to it.

And so, as we invite you up stage, the DJ will play some music for you as you come to take your seat. So coming up stage-faced, we do have Mr. Dawid Gawaseb, Senior Youth Officer from Namibia. ...all your money, V, Netumbo, August, Tutoni, That is Namibia for you, please take your seat.

That is Namibia from the land of vast opportunities and strategic... Please take a seat. That is Namibia, from the land of vast opportunities and strategic Atlantic coastline. Let us hear what Namibia has to offer to our young African entrepreneurs today.
I'll allow my co-host to invite the next country. I don't think you're ready for this one. Of course, I'm going to be biased because that's where I come from.

And our representative, sir, please, don't let me down. At this point in time, we are going to have... Ah, guys, I'm excited. The permanent secretary for the Ministry of Youth and Sport, representing Zambia.

And as you all know it, Zambia is positioned at the crossroads of southern, central and eastern Africa. Zambia has opportunities across agriculture, mining, manufacturing, tourism, technology and regional trade. Zambia, this is your moment.
I know. Yes, I told you guys, I told you. That is our permanent secretary, Mr. Congratulation.
And young people, if you're a young creative, you have yourself a mentor just right in front of you. I have so much to learn from him. Thank you very much.
Over to you. Thank you so much, Hope. And coming up next is a country known for its natural resources, economic potential and drive to diversity, Botswana.
What is your offer to Africa's youth today? Coming up is Miss Natasha Rampa, permanent secretary for the Ministry of Youth and Gender Affairs. Up next, our neighbors. It's the central part of Zambia.
They are just a capital city or somewhere, just an extension, Zambia extension. But we love them. They are our brothers and sisters.
Up next, we have the warm heart of Africa. That is Malawi, who are going to come up here and tell us the opportunities that lie in their country. Such a beautiful country of Malawi, Zambia extension.
We love you guys. At this point, we're going to have Miss Judith Mususa, who is the Director of Youth, Ministry of Youth, Sports and Culture in Malawi. Thank you so much, Malawi.

Coming up next is one of the continent's largest and most diversified economies with extensive industrial, financial and innovation ecosystems, South Africa. What is your offer to the next generation of African entrepreneurs? Coming up, we have Mr. Emmanuel Nganaga, Director of Youth, Legislation and Policy. I'm so glad I'm not part of the jury because I would have been voting best of the songs and the dances.

At this point, we're going to transition into a country with regional connections and opportunities for enterprise, innovation and trade, Eswatini. What do you have for the young people? And Eswatini is going to be pitched, the Kingdom of Eswatini is going to be pitched by the Chief Executive Officer of the Eswatini National Youth Council, Mr. Lwazi Mamba. Thank you so much, Eswatini.

Coming up next is a country with immense entrepreneurial energy and opportunities in agriculture, manufacturing, mining and services, the land of my father, Zimbabwe. Come and make the case for your country. Okay, I think I need to charge Zimbabwe for one thing.

You came with a very big delegation. Text them, let them come up and fill the room and for the rest of us, text your bestie to come in the room so that we have fun together. The next country up is from the Mountain Kingdom with opportunities in agriculture, textiles, tourism and emerging enterprises.
Who can guess that? Who can guess that? Great, you're all right. At this point in time, I'm going to call upon the Honorable Minister who is pitching the land of Lesotho. Okay.

That is so amazing. Just before they even tell us their countries, we already know that we can move, right? Great. So, at this particular point in time, please, to our presenters, let's be mindful of time because young people don't buy into speeches.

We buy into what looks good for us. So, we are going to go straight in and I'm going to kindly ask that even as you come up here to pitch, you look, after you speak, you could be looking at our timekeeper who's just seated right in front of you with the HP laptop. He'll be giving you some tips on how much time you're remaining with.
Are we ready? Are we ready? Young people, are we ready to vote? Perfect. We're going to have Namibia come up first. A round of applause.
A round of applause for Namibia. It's about to go down. It's microphone check.
Thank you very much. Good morning, distinguished delegates, ministers, private sector leaders, and above all, our young people of Africa, SADC in particular. Halala the youth.
Halala. Africa is the youngest continent, a median age of 19 and around 530 million people aged between 15 and 35 years. With my experience, I know our challenge is not talent.
It is the pathways. Trade is one of the strongest of them. And in the next five minutes, Namibia will show you ours.

A young entrepreneur who sells his or her maize only at home is limited to a size of a home market. Connected to Africa continental free trade area, that same entrepreneur can reach about 1.3 billion people and a combined GDP of about 3.2 trillion U.S. dollars. Can you imagine? The World Bank estimates that full implementation of AFTA could raise Africa's income by 450 billion U.S. dollars.

About 7% more by 2035. Further analysis shows that if we have deeper investment and protocol reforms, we could have easily upped the points by 18 million new jobs up to 571 billion U.S. dollars. So why trade matters for youth? These gains are not automatic, mind you.

They depend on implementation and on young people being able to use the market. That is why this very session matters the most. Why you must invest in Namibia? Namibia is a stable democracy with peace and tranquility with our mother president leading us.
We have ratified the AFTA in 2019 and already in 2025 we have launched the first export consignment under it from our port of Wallfish Bay. 45,000 tons to Nigeria. This is salt, our salt.

The U.N. Economic Commission for Africa has called our roads in Wallfish Bay as a strategic gateway to the regional and continental trade. For the young trader in southern Africa, that means a road to the wide Atlantic and the world markets. You may ask for concrete offers.

So here are just a few of them. First one, skills. For the new energy economy, which is booming in Namibia, the youth, our youth, sorry, pardon me, our youth for green hydrogen scholarships fund, which is technical training for youth aged between 18 and 35 in solar installation, the wind turbine servicing, welding and industrial electrics, and the list goes on.

Our cabinet furthermore has approved a local content policy for our upstream oil gas sector covering procurement, employment, and skills so that young Namibians and equally young Africans and their businesses can supply the industry as it grows. The most important one, finance. The National Youth Development Fund, together with the government SME financing, the youth entrepreneurship strategy brings venture capital fund and credit guarantee schemes and training coupled with mentorship.

So allow me in conclusion, citing the time, young Africans, if you want a place where opportunities meets ambition, regional connectivity meets innovation, Namibia is ready to partner with you. Africa's greatest advantage lies beyond our minerals, our energy, our land. It is our young people.

Let us treat after not just as a trade agreement, but as a platform for youth entrepreneurship and job creation. Finally, come trade with Namibia, invest with Namibia, innovate with Namibia, grow with Namibia. Alala, the youth of Africa, alala.
Thank you very much. Come on, Africa. We can do better than that.

A round of applause for Namibia. We have had the opportunities for our young people in Namibia have been presented. Would you move to Namibia as a young person in lieu of what has just been presented before us? That is something for you to think about.
Coming up next, we have Botswana to come and pitch your country. So the lyrics to this song say, it means that's where we're heading. That is where we are going, Africa.
The sky is not the limit. It is beyond there. Young people of Africa, that is our greeting in Setswana.
